summary:
## The Core Pillars of Effective Shooting

A good shot in Rocket League is defined by two fundamental factors: **time** and **readability**. Your goal as an attacker is to minimize both of these factors to give the defender the smallest possible chance of making a save.

> [!NOTE]
> Visualize these factors as two buckets. A perfect shot keeps both the 'Time' bucket and the 'Readability' bucket as empty as possible.

## Breaking Down the Pillars

### The 'Time' Factor
The total time from your touch to the ball crossing the goal line is determined by two components:

*   **Shot Speed (Powershots)**: Faster shots reduce the defender's reaction time. Consistently generating power is a crucial skill.
*   **Distance (Spacing)**: Shooting from closer to the net naturally reduces the ball's travel time.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> There is a risk-reward balance with spacing. Getting closer to the net increases the risk that a defender will challenge and block the shot before you can even take it. The key is finding the sweet spot.

### The 'Readability' Factor
This factor is a measure of how predictable your attack is. It relates directly to your creativity.

*   **Creativity**: This is your ability to score in many different ways from the same or similar starting positions. The more shot options you have in your arsenal (flicks, fakes, air dribbles, ground shots), the harder you are to read.

## How to Diagnose and Train Your Weaknesses

### Are Your Powershots Weak?
*   **Symptom**: Your shots feel slow, or you're not impressed with the power you generate compared to high-level players.
*   **Solution**: Use the custom **Powershot Training Pack** provided in the video. Focus only on hitting the ball as hard as possible, aiming for the speed targets mentioned.
*   > [!TIP]
> To generate maximum power, flip into the ball with your car's nose just *before* making contact.

### Is Your Spacing Poor?
*   **Symptom**: You have a low shooting percentage (e.g., 1 goal on 6 shots). This often means you're taking shots from too far away, giving the defender ample time to react.
*   **Solution**: Play **1v1s**. This mode provides the most opportunities to practice reading an opponent's defensive positioning.
*   **Objective**: Learn to recognize opponent patterns. Shoot in the "sweet spot"—as close as you can get to the goal without being challenged.

### Do You Lack Creativity?
*   **Symptom**: In 1v1s, you take an early lead but then lose as the game goes on. This suggests your opponent has adapted to your limited, predictable playstyle.
*   **Solution**: Use the custom **Creativity Training Pack** provided in the video.
*   **Objective**: For each shot in the pack, practice scoring in as many different ways as you can (e.g., immediate shot, hook shot, fake-to-flick, backboard double tap, air dribble). Don't just practice what you're good at.
*   > [!IMPORTANT]
> The key to unpredictability isn't being spontaneous. It's about having a wide range of practiced skills that you can deploy at will.
transcription:
## A New Perspective on Shooting

By the end of this video, the way you view shooting in Rocket League will be completely different from the way you see it right now. So stay tuned.

Shooting in Rocket League is one of the most under analyzed aspects in the game. Mainly because it’s just so incredibly complex and so hard to break down into simple terms. And I’m not just talking about powershots, I’m talking about shooting in the greater picture. Powershots are a very specific aspect within shooting that’s a much easier concept to teach but shooting as a whole is incredibly complicated.

Because of this, most people just learn how to make good shots naturally through trial and error of playing the game or in training packs. That’s how I learned it and that’s how pretty much everyone in the playerbase has learned it up until this point. But with this new perspective I’m about to give you, you’ll be able to see shooting for what it really is and use that to your advantage against everyone else that still sees it the way you do right now.

So I’ll first begin by explaining the foundation of what makes a shot good in the first place compared to a bad shot, and then I’ll explain how you can use that knowledge to choose exactly how you should practice in order to improve your shooting as fast as possible. Real quick, let me warn you that I’m going to throw a lot of information at you but please stick with me because I’m going to make this thing go full circle by the end and once I'm all finished you’ll be like, “Oh it makes sense now.” So just be patient with me.

## The Two Pillars: Time & Readability

For the sake of simplicity, all the examples I’ll give for this will be when there’s one defender all the way back and there’s one attacker starting from wherever on the field.

Alright, almost everyone can look at a shot and decide if it was good or bad. Like here obviously this is an example of a good shot, and this is an example of a bad shot. I’m sure you’re capable of noticing that too. But what about these shots makes them good or bad? Well, simple enough, there’s 2 main factors that go into it.

The first one is the time from when the ball leaves your car to when it reaches the goal, so we’ll just call that the time. And the second one is the readability. So basically just how easy it is for the defender to tell what the attacker is going to do and where they’re going to place it. These are the two main factors that determine whether an attack is good or bad. You want to make your shot have the least amount of time and the least amount of readability as possible. The less these 2 buckets are filled, the smaller chance the defender has at saving it.

A cool way to visualize this is by taking the total of each of these buckets and placing it into its own separate thing. Whether the shot goes in or not may depend on the rank or skill level of your opponent. But regardless of the opponent's skill, you still want to keep these as empty as possible. You want to make your attack as unreadable as you can while also lowering the time between your hit and when it reaches the goal.

Now, there are some exceptions to this that make it slightly more complicated. For example, the time factor depends on two things which are your distance from the goal and the speed of your shot. Theoretically, you could reduce the time by literally just reducing the distance to the goal to be right next to it. So technically, the time would be at almost zero but we all know it’s not that simple. The closer you get to the goal before taking your shot, the higher the risk is that the defender will push out and cut it off before you even shoot it. So that’s something to be aware of.

As for the readability factor, what makes a shot readable actually depends on how creative you are as a player. This is something almost everybody struggles with. It’s a really bad habit to just hop into freeplay and go for air dribbles over and over again if you’re already decent at them. You need to mix it up a bit. If you only practice a few different types of attacks, those are the only ones you’re going to be good at when you actually get in game and your opponents are going to realize that and have a pretty easy time reading you since you’ve only got a few different types of shots in your repertoire. So being creative is basically being able to score in all sorts of different ways. That’s why it relates to how readable you are.

## Applying the Framework & Diagnosing Weaknesses

Now, with this system, you can pretty much rank any type of attack or offensive mechanic in the game on how effective it will be. For example, mind games, if done correctly, would probably be a completely empty bucket on the readability but decently full on the time, since the ball isn’t going to be going very fast but it’s really hard to tell what the shooter is going to do. Whereas something like just a good strong powershot from somewhat close range would be a mostly empty bucket on the time but decently full on readability, simply because the defender probably knows where it’s going but they just won’t be able to get to it in time.

Something like a ceiling shot or a flip reset is probably mostly empty on both because you can use your flip at any moment making it really hard to read and you can get a decent amount of power if you do it right. The only type of attack that doesn’t really fall into this analogy is something related to a bump play but that’s not really about the shot itself. It’s more just about getting a solid bump so that’s just its own thing.

Alright. We’ve broken down the main factors that make a shot good or bad. Now that we’ve done this, you can actually work specifically on whichever aspect you think you struggle with the most. Whether it be creativity, spacing, or powershots. So I’m now going to cover what it looks like to be struggling with one of these aspects and how you should practice to improve that aspect of your shooting.

## Training Your Powershots for Speed

Let’s begin by looking at the time bucket. We’ll talk about powershots first which relates to speed. Most of the time, you can tell you’re not getting enough power on your shots just by playing the game. But if you’re still unsure, watch some gameplay of a high level player and see if you’re impressed by the amount of power they’re generating from their shots. You’ll probably be impressed by their gameplay as a whole anyway but try and drown out everything aside from the power of their touches. If it looks like they’re hitting the ball with power that doesn’t exactly make sense to you, you definitely need to work on your powershots.

To practice this, I created a training pack that I believe is the best for practicing to get that power specifically instead of focusing on a ton of things at once like shot placement, hitting it early, and power. The code is on screen now and in the description and I’ll go over how you’re supposed to complete this pack real quick. Okay.

The main idea for these shots is to try and hit it as hard as possible by of course flipping into it with your nose. Make sure you flip just before you hit the ball to generate the most power instead of flipping just after. And don’t worry about your shot placement. Only worry about how hard you're hitting the ball for this drill.

For shot number one, the fastest I could get it to go is about 118 so try and get as close to that as you can. Even if you can’t get it that fast, that should give you an idea for what you’re capable of.

For shot number 2, the fastest I could get it was about 115 so if you can get it close to that then you’re doing it perfectly.

For shot 3, I could get to about 109.

For shot 4, the fastest I could get was 113 and it definitely helps to put a little bit of air roll into it for this one.

For shot 5, it’s best to try and hit it immediately after it touches the ground there on that bounce and I was able to make it go 111 kilometers an hour.

And for shot 6, I could get it to go 117.

So again, if you’re struggling with powershots, try out this training pack and aim for those speeds I mentioned for each shot. If you want to learn more about generating power in your shots, there are plenty of great tutorials out there and I may even end up making one of my own in the future to go more in depth.

## Mastering Spacing & Decision Making

Now, on the other side of the bucket is spacing which relates to distance. Spacing is a pretty broad topic because it includes your teammates as well as your opponents but since this video is about shooting, we’re only going to talk about how it includes your opponents.

The best way to visualize spacing with your opponents is through that diagram I showed earlier about the risk of your opponent cutting you off increasing as you get closer to the net. Basically, a shot with really good spacing is one that gets as close to the net as possible without the opponent cutting it off. Remember, you want to lower that time between your hit and the goal to be as short as possible and lowering your distance to the goal is one way of doing that. But it does come at the cost of risking the opponent pushing the ball early, so you have to find the perfect balance to where you’re close to the goal but not too close to where the opponent can cut it off.

A sign that you’re struggling with spacing is if you have a low shooting percentage so like if you have 1 goal with 6 shots. A lot of the time that means you’re taking shots from too far away and the defender has a ton of time to read your hit and save it. The best way to improve your spacing with your opponents is simply by playing 1s. In 1s, you’ll get, by far, the most opportunities to read your opponent on defense as possible. As you’re playing, try and notice some patterns for what they normally do when they’re about to cut you off. When you think they’re about to push you, that’s when you shoot. You can use this method of recognizing patterns to learn spacing in any mode but you get the most opportunities for it in 1s. So if you’re trying to learn it the fastest, 1s is the best place to do it.

And I’ll say it again, remember that the objective is to shoot during that sweet spot where you’re close to their goal but they aren’t pushing you yet.

## Becoming Unpredictable with Creativity

Finally, we’ve got creativity. This of course relates to your readability bucket. As I mentioned, your readability strongly correlates to how confident you are with different types of shots starting from the same point.

So basically, if you find yourself in this position at one point in the game, you might just keep dribbling and go for a flick and score off of it. But if you find yourself in that same position later on, you don’t want to do that exact same thing because if your opponent is smart, they’re going to be expecting it. Instead, you should try something different like dropping it down and going for a hook shot or something. The more types of shots you have up your sleeve, the harder it is for the opponent to read you.

A sign that you struggle with creativity is if when you play 1s, you usually take early leads in the beginning but you end up losing in the end. The cause for that could be you totally choking under pressure every time or the opponent is just adapting to your playstyle and can read your attacks way easier by the end of the game. Creativity is probably the most underrated skill to have among non-GCs.

If you struggle with creativity, which chances are you do, then I’ve created a training pack that will help you take different types of shots from the same situation. Once again, the code is on screen now and in the description. For this pack, your objective is to hit each shot in as many different ways as possible. For example, in this first one I can take the shot immediately and place it on the right side of the net or I could do it on the left side. I could also do a hook shot and place that wherever I want. I can fake the hook shot and then do a touch and flick. I can hit it off the backboard and double tap it in. Or I could completely not hit it at all at first and take it up the wall for a ceiling shot or air dribble. You see what I mean? There’s so many different ways I could take this shot.

When you’re practicing this, you want to be good at as many of these as you can. The more tricks you have up your sleeve, the harder it is for the opponent to prepare themself for what you’re about to do. There’s 10 shots in this pack and I’m not going to go over all of them but I think you get the idea of how many different ways there are to take these shots. Don’t only practice what you find fun or only what you’re already good at. Practice everything that you could legitimately use in a game. You’ll immediately notice yourself scoring more often when you shoot and you’ll leave the defenders lost as to where you’re going to place it and even what you’re going to do entirely.

The key to unpredictability is not making your decisions spontaneous. It’s about having a wide range of skills that you can use at any moment you want. Taking these shots in multiple different ways is the best way to get in the mentality of doing things differently each time so you won’t be as readable to the defenders.

## Recap: The Complete Shooting Framework

So to recap what we covered and bring this whole thing full circle, we began by talking about what makes a shot good or bad and determined that it comes down to time and readability. But you can break that down even further to where time is about speed and distance and readability is about creativity including shot placement. Then we talked about how you can determine which of those aspects you struggle with the most and what you can do to improve those aspects.

I hope you learned something and enjoyed this. If you did, please be sure to like the video and hit subscribe so you don’t miss out on future videos like this one. Other than that, thank you for watching, and I’ll see you later!
